answer: Three issues. (1) Shares are priced from the raw token balance with no virtual offset or minimum, so a first depositor can mint 1 wei of shares, transfer assets straight in, and make the next deposit round down to zero shares, then redeem everything. (2) `claimFees` has no caller check and takes any `to`, so anyone can take the treasury's accrued fees. (3) `deposit` sets `mark` to the current price without calling `chargeFee` first, so any deposit, even 1 wei, erases the fee owed on the gain since the last charge.
grading: judge: Passes only if the reply names all three: (1) first-depositor share inflation, meaning shares priced from the raw balance let a tiny first deposit plus a direct transfer make later deposits mint zero or too few shares; (2) `claimFees` lacks access control or lets the caller pick `to`, so anyone can take the treasury's fees; (3) `deposit` resets `mark` to the current price without charging the fee first, so the treasury loses the fee on gains since the last charge. Fails if any of the three is missing or only hinted at without the mechanism, or if the reply reports as a vulnerability something that is not one here, for example reentrancy through the ERC20 transfers, `claimFees` being re-enterable, `redeem` paying out the treasury's fees, or `redeem` skipping the fee charge. The nit rule above applies.

answer: Three issues. (1) `deposit` pulls the USDC in before pricing the shares, so `totalAssets()` already counts the deposit and the depositor is minted `amount * s / (assets + amount)` instead of `amount * s / assets`; 1,000 USDC into a 1,000-share, 1,000 USDC vault mints 500 shares worth about 667 USDC. (2) `redeem` passes an asset amount to `pool.redeem`, which takes pool shares; once a pool share is worth more than 1 USDC each redeemer is overpaid out of the other holders' backing (it should be `pool.withdraw(amount, ...)`). (3) Unclaimed gauge rewards are not in `totalAssets()` and neither `deposit` nor `redeem` harvests first, so anyone can deposit, call `harvest()` and take a share of rewards earned before they joined, while a redeemer before a harvest forfeits rewards they earned.
grading: judge: Passes only if the reply names all three: (1) `deposit` computes shares after the USDC transfer, so `totalAssets()` includes the deposit and the depositor gets too few shares; (2) `redeem` passes an asset amount to `pool.redeem`, which expects pool shares, so payouts are wrong (overpaid while a pool share is worth more than 1 USDC); (3) pending gauge rewards are excluded from `totalAssets()` and `deposit`/`redeem` do not harvest first, so a deposit just before `harvest()` takes rewards earned by existing holders (or a redeem before it loses them). Fails if any of the three is missing or only hinted at without the mechanism, or if the reply reports as a vulnerability something that is not one here, for example first-depositor inflation (the burned 1,000 USDC launch deposit rules it out), reentrancy through USDC or the pool, the unlimited approval to the trusted pool, or `redeem` rounding in the user's favour. The nit rule above applies.

answer: Three issues. (1) `depositFor` accepts any target and any amount, including zero, and stamps `lastDeposit[a] = block.number`, so anyone can make a user's `withdraw` revert in every block by depositing nothing for them first. (2) `liquidate` pushes the leftover ETH to the borrower with `Address.sendValue`, which reverts when the receiver rejects ETH, so a borrower contract can make its own liquidation impossible and leave bad debt (this holds even when the leftover is zero). (3) `liquidate` clears the position's debt but never lowers `totalDebt`, unlike `repay`, so liquidated debt keeps filling the 10,000,000 cap until nobody can borrow.
grading: judge: Passes only if the reply names all three: (1) anyone can call `depositFor` for another user, even with zero ETH, to reset that user's `lastDeposit` and block their `withdraw` (griefing or front-running the same-block rule); (2) the leftover ETH is pushed to the borrower during `liquidate`, so a borrower contract that rejects ETH blocks its own liquidation; (3) `liquidate` does not reduce `totalDebt`, so the global cap fills with debt that no longer exists and borrowing eventually stops. Fails if any of the three is missing or only hinted at without the mechanism, or if the reply reports as a vulnerability something that is not one here, for example reentrancy in `withdraw` or `liquidate` (state is cleared before each send), a liquidator taking more than the position's ETH, `repay` letting someone reduce another user's debt, or oracle manipulation (the oracle is trusted). Design remarks such as full-only liquidation, no bad-debt handling for positions under water, or withdrawals needing zero debt count as nits. The nit rule above applies.

answer: Three issues. (1) `setProtocol` has no access check, so anyone can point the protocol fee at themselves (or at a contract that rejects ETH and stops all buys). (2) `sell` pushes the subject's fee to the subject with `Address.sendValue`, so a subject that is a contract can stop accepting ETH and make every holder's sell revert, trapping the ETH they paid. (3) `sell` deducts 10% from the seller but pays out only the subject's 5%; the protocol's 5% of every sell stays in the contract with no way to withdraw it.
grading: judge: Passes only if the reply names all three: (1) `setProtocol` has no access control, so anyone can redirect (or block) the protocol fee; (2) `sell` pushes the subject's fee to the subject, so a subject contract that rejects ETH blocks all sells of its keys and traps holders' funds; (3) on `sell` the protocol's 5% is deducted from the seller but never sent anywhere, so it is stuck in the contract. Fails if any of the three is missing or only hinted at without the mechanism, or if the reply reports as a vulnerability something that is not one here, for example reentrancy in `buy` or `sell` (state is updated before each send), buyers overpaying or being sandwiched (the exact `msg.value` check rejects a moved price), or an unpayable curve because the first key is free. Design remarks such as the first key being free and unsellable count as nits. The nit rule above applies.

answer: Two issues. (1) The 5,000,000 USDC limit is checked against `totalSupply()`, which counts shares; once interest lifts the share price above 1 USDC the pool accepts more than 5,000,000 USDC (a year at 10% on an 80% drawn pool already lets in over 5.3 million). (2) `borrow` checks the one-fifth cash rule before lending, so the rule constrains the state before the draw, not after it: a single `borrow` can take all of the pool's cash, and lenders cannot redeem.
grading: judge: Passes only if the reply names both: (1) the deposit cap compares the share supply (`totalSupply()`) with a USDC amount, so once shares are worth more than 1 USDC the pool accepts more than 5,000,000 USDC; (2) the cash-reserve check in `borrow` runs before the loan is added and sent, so one borrow can drain the cash below a fifth (to zero) and block redemptions. Fails if either is missing or only hinted at without the mechanism, or if the reply reports as a vulnerability something that is not one here, for example first-depositor inflation (the launch shares are burned), reentrancy through `usdc`, `deposit` minting before the transfer letting a depositor keep shares without paying (the whole call reverts), interest being lost or doubled by `accrue`, or a stranger borrowing. Remarks that the borrower may never repay, that redemptions wait for cash, that interest compounds per call, or that a full repayment can be made to revert by a 1-unit repayment placed in front of it count as nits. The nit rule above applies.

answer: Three issues. (1) `blockLender` calls `_escrow(lender, borrower)`, but `_escrow` takes `(address b, address a)` and builds `Escrow(b, a, ...)` with `b` as the borrower and `a` as the account, so the escrow's account is the real borrower; since the borrower is not sanctioned, anyone can call `release` and the sanctioned lender's tokens go to the borrower. (2) `e.codehash == bytes32(0)` is not a "no contract here" test: an address that holds ETH but no code has codehash `keccak256("")`, so anyone who sends 1 wei to the predicted escrow address makes `_escrow` skip the deployment, and the lender's tokens are moved to an address with no code, where nothing can ever move them (`e.code.length == 0` is the right test). (3) Market tokens move by plain ERC20 transfers that never consult `sanctions`, so a sanctioned lender can move the balance to a fresh address before (or instead of) being blocked, and anyone can send tokens to sanctioned accounts; the escrow then catches nothing.
grading: judge: Passes only if the reply names all three: (1) `blockLender` passes `(lender, borrower)` to `_escrow(b, a)`, so the escrow's borrower and account are swapped and the lender's tokens can be released to the borrower; (2) the `codehash == bytes32(0)` existence check is wrong for an address that already holds ETH, so a 1 wei transfer to the predicted address skips the escrow deployment and the tokens are sent to a codeless address and lost; (3) market-token transfers do not check sanctions, so a sanctioned lender can move tokens to another address and escape the block (or receive them). Fails if any of the three is missing or only hinted at without the mechanism, or if the reply reports as a vulnerability something that is not one here, for example someone deploying different code at the escrow address, `blockLender` being callable by anyone (only sanctioned lenders can be blocked), the borrower's early release paying anyone but the escrow's account, or reentrancy through the market token. A reply that blames `release` being callable by anyone, or the borrower override, for the loss in issue 1 without naming the swapped arguments does not name issue 1. The nit rule above applies.
